approved: Treasury Laws Amendment (Australian Consumer Law Review) Bill 2018
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would change consumer protection rules to make them clearer and stronger.
It would amend the ASIC Act, the Australian Consumer Law and the Competition and Consumer Act to put into action proposals from a 2017 review.
The amendments cover areas such as guarantees on goods and services, door-to-door sales, product safety, fake billing, unfair business behaviour, pricing and unfair contract terms.
The bill would clarify and strengthen protections for consumers.
It would help consumers and businesses understand their rights and obligations.
The changes would make the consumer protection system able to handle new issues.

The bill implements recommendations from the Australian Consumer Law Review, including expanding 'follow on' provisions for private litigants, extending unconscionable conduct protections to publicly listed companies, requiring online retailers to include pre‑selected fees in the headline price, and strengthening the ACCC’s product‑safety information‑gathering powers.

The speaker argued that Australian competition law should be strengthened to include a provision like Europe's, which prohibits dominant companies from limiting production to the prejudice of consumers—citing AGL's planned closure of the Liddell coal-fired power station as an example of such anti-competitive conduct.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Australian Consumer Law Review) Bill 2018 but argued that consumer laws still have gaps, citing exploitation by payday lenders, car manufacturers, airlines, insurers, telcos, private health insurers, and energy providers, and specifically criticised Toys R Us administrators McGrathNicol for requiring gift card holders to spend double the value of their cards.

The government proposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Australian Consumer Law Review) Bill 2018 to strengthen consumer protections across 11 schedules, including easing evidentiary requirements for private litigants, extending unconscionable conduct protections to publicly listed companies, enhancing online price transparency, and broadening the ACCC's product safety information powers.

The government moved an amendment to the Treasury Laws Amendment (Australian Consumer Law Review) Bill 2018, inserting new subsections to section 13 that allow ASIC to investigate financial product or small business contracts to determine whether to apply to the Court under section 12GND.
